The Maiden Bursary

By: Tarryn Crossman | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We look at the newest bursary to be launched by the Uthukela municipality, the Maiden bursary is awarded to virgins only

Summary:
When the Uthukela Municipality launched it new maiden bursary, exclusively for virgins, South Africans were up in arms. Many felt that virginity testing is a patriarchal tradition and that a woman’s right to an eduction should not be directly linked to her virginity. But on the other hand the cultural practice of virginity testing has been around for centuries and in KZN many girls have already pledged to be virgins and are undergoing virginity testing regularly. Mayor Mazibuko feels strongly that the bursary will inspired girls to stay virgins and therefore reduce the spread of HIV and teenage pregnancy cases.

This story looks at two girls who received the bursary and have proudly pledged their virginity. We find out what their circumstance are, how they feel about doing regular virginity testing and getting the bursary. We also meet the elders from both villages who put the girls forward for the bursary and will be doing the regular testing. These elders are solely responsible to report on the girls virginity status to the municipality, every varsity holiday.

We also speak to Nomboniso Gasa, an author and professor on politics and gender studies. She feels that the intentions behind the bursary are good, but is strongly apposed to a woman’s virginity being aligned to her right to an education. She is also very concerned about this bursary in relation to the high cases of sexual assault on woman in South Africa.

At the end of the piece the audience will have made an emotional connection with the girls who have received the bursary. They will have heard both what makes this a genius idea and how this is a step backwards for woman’s rights in South Africa. And then they can make their own minds up.

Opening scene girls packing their bags to go to varsity, books, clothes. Establish their homes

Press Release:


Virginity and Education
Local and international outrage followed the announcement of a controversial Maiden Bursary fund established by KZN’s Uthukela Municipality. Young girls have an opportunity to access funding for their tertiary education if they submit to yearly virginity testing. Carte Blanche asks: should a woman’s right to education be linked to her virginity?


Script:


Time code CHARACTER/VISUAL
1 00:00 Maidens gathering in KZN Maidens singing and dancing

V/O: Thabelihle: I’m from Ladysmith Zolisha, a rural area. Many of the girls are unemployed and others are just working at the farm and they earn peanuts for a living. It’s not easy.
2 00:27 Thabelihle I don’t want to end up like the other girls because I want to achieve my goals and do what will make this rural area change.
3 00:45 Claire Link I am in the heart of Zulu land where virginity testing is a widely accepted cultural practice. So when the Uthukela district municipality launched a higher education bursary specifically for virgins called “The maiden bursary”. It could not have foreseen the overwhelming criticism and controversy it would spark both locally and internationally.
4 01:07 Claire Voice V/O: This bursary is the brainchild of Uthukela District mayor, Dude Mazibuko and is available for Tertiary education for girls in five local Municipalities including Ladysmith.
5 01:15 Mayor dude mazibuko Let us start about the bursaries that the municipality offer. Because the maiden is just one of the four categories that the municipality has. The maiden bursary is not only about virginity. Being a maiden, it means you have a matron who is taking care of you and teaching you to grow up and be a responsible adult. You also attend the reed dance and you take part in all the activities.
6 01:51 Claire asks question What are the other criteria that this bursary looks at?
7 01:53 Mayor dude mazibuko answers It’s the normal criteria for everyone. You must be the resident of the Uthukela district municipality. You must be from a destitute family. Produce your ID and you must show us that you have been accepted to the institution of higher learning. For the maidens you then need to produce the certificate to show that you are a maiden. You regularly attend the reed dance.
8 02:25 Mayor dude mazibuko The certificate that you need to submit comes from the matron.
9 02:31 Dudu Zwane Good afternoon young ladies.
10 02:40 Claire link asks question Are you saying that your virginity testing is 100% correct? Because doctors say that there is no scientific proof of that. They don’t know what you as a matron are looking at. Do you always get it right?
11 02:53 Dudu Zwane answers It is 100% correct because you can see a vagina that is active. Because this thing is practical. You can’t tell it or discuss about it, you can’t.
12 03:06 Dudu Zwane speaks to a crowd What are the preventions of HIV, if you still remember?

13 03:10 Child in the crowd responds You must use a condom.
14 03:13 Dudu Zwane You must use a condom. Yes. You must abstain from sex. And you must be faithful. And which one are you using? Which method?
15 03:23 Second child in crowd responds Abstaining.
16 03:26 Dudu Zwane You are using abstaining. Okay, you’ll have a problem if you fall pregnant now. So what are you going to do? You are going to abstain. You must always try to develop the skills to say no. you must be so assertive. If you don’t sleep around with boys it means that you are pure. Because you have just kept your virginity.
17 03:52 Claire Link asks question So, if she stops being a virgin while she has got the bursary what happens?
18 03:56 Mayor dude mazibuko answers The bursary lasts for a year. You know, right now as a municipality we are already paying for all those who were awarded bursaries. So, it’s immaterial to us. We will only see you next year when you come and reapply.
19 04:14 Claire Link asks question Are they not going to be tested this year?
20 04:16 Mayor dude mazibuko answers No.
21 04:18 Claire Voice V/O: Thabelihle is one of the 16 maidens to receive this bursary for her first year of tertiary education in 2016.
22 04:24 Thabelihle Dlodlo Yes, since I was nine years old I followed the virginity testing and now I am eighteen years old.
23 04:31 Thabelihle Dlodlo voice V/O: Virginity testing is when we lie down on the mats and the mother will check you. It’s private because you come with your mother and not everyone will just look at you.
24 04:42 Thabelihle Dlodlo We are not forced by our parents or our grandmothers. We love it from our hearts and no one forces us. There’s no “do this”, “do virginity testing”. No, we are not invaded in our privacies and we enjoy it a lot.
25 04: 57 Nomboniso Gasa Virginity testing is a very old practise. It’s basically about control of women’s sexuality. It is not only an African practise. Because virginity testing is part of a larger practise and patriarchal practise of control of women’s sexuality and body’s.
26 05:30 Dudu Zwane What happens at school especially as you are coming from a poor family? What has happened at school?
27 05:35 Child in crowd answers They are dating with the teachers and they are sleeping with them just because they want money.
28 05:42 Dudu Zwane Ya, how old are these boyfriends of them?
29 05:46 Child in crowd answers Maybe they’re like fourteen or thirty something
30 05:48 Dudu Zwane People who are working? People who have got cars?
31 05:52 Child in crowd answers They are starting from twelve years old, even in primary schools they are with older men.
Dudu Zwane: Because they want money?
Child: Yes
32 06:03 Mayor dude mazibuko If you see a twelve year old pregnant, you just ask yourself where is this country going to.
33 06:11 Dudu Zwana Why you say you don’t want to fall pregnant now.
34 06:14 Thabelihle Dlodlo A child has many expenses especially we are not working and our parents are not of a good and rich family. So that is why we choose to abstain so that we cannot extend expenses for our parents.
35 06:26 Claire Link Nationally teen pregnancies have reached alarming numbers. In KwaZulu Natal alone in 2015, 3000 school going teenagers fell pregnant. Of that number a whopping 84 were primary school pupils. And KwaZulu Natal has the highest HIV infection rate in the country.
36 06:45 Mayor dude mazibuko The reason why we introduced this maiden bursary, we want to motivate them. So that we can decrease the early teenage pregnancies and the infection of HIV and AIDS in the district because the statistics are very high. We want them to go beyond that, to have careers, to go and study so that they can be self-sustained.
37 07:10 Nomboniso Gasa I hear where the municipality is coming from. What they think they’re trying to do but programs like this, they put it all on this one woman. You can apply for catagories of bursary as a young man but there is one that is meant for girls. Because they have to prove themselves that they are pure. But you don’t have to. I think focussing on young women is a problem. There’s a problem in burdening women with messages that they and they alone are responsible for their sexual health in their relationships and for the sexual health in society.
38 07:57 Claire Link Voice V/O: Because this bursary requires woman to disclose their sexual history many have argued that it goes against the constitution and therefore the commission for gender equality have opened an investigation. The findings of which should be out by mid-march this year
39 08:13 Mayor dude mazibuko We have said you know, we believe that the municipality, that we haven’t done anything wrong and I think the investigation by the gender commission will be just highlighting the loop holes and hopefully they will tell us what we need to do in order to ensure that there are no loop holes in the bursary scheme that we are offering.
40 08:42 Nomboniso Gasa It’s against the constitution. We live in a society that is based on the constitution and the constitution secular. South Africa is defined in the constitution as a secular country. I think it’s short sighted. I think a bursary like that; from a government entity has no space in South Africa.
41 09:03 Mayor dude mazibuko The funniest part is if you talk to the resident they are very happy about this bursary and they would want it to continue. But when you talk to someone maybe who doesn’t understand it clearly, that is when you find a problem and I think for us because we are serving the community we are not saying we are going to break the law. The laws of the country or the constitution in the interest of serving the community of Uthukela. But, the fact remains that the residents, the communities here loved the idea.
42 09:49 Thabelihle Dlodlo In 2021 I’ll be finishing my degree. I want to be a lecturer in university and just conquer the world, to travel the world and know every country that I don’t know right now.
43 10:03 Claire Link Being here in this community, I can understand why being a maiden is something special and to be celebrated. But I am also deeply conflicted about what patriarchal message is being sent out to both men and women.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We look at the newest bursary to be launched by the Uthukela municipality, the Maiden bursary is awarded to virgins only
metadata.Summary: When the Uthukela Municipality launched it new maiden bursary, exclusively for virgins, South Africans were up in arms. Many felt that virginity testing is a patriarchal tradition and that a woman’s right to an eduction should not be directly linked to her virginity. But on the other hand the cultural practice of virginity testing has been around for centuries and in KZN many girls have already pledged to be virgins and are undergoing virginity testing regularly. Mayor Mazibuko feels strongly that the bursary will inspired girls to stay virgins and therefore reduce the spread of HIV and teenage pregnancy cases. This story looks at two girls who received the bursary and have proudly pledged their virginity. We find out what their circumstance are, how they feel about doing regular virginity testing and getting the bursary. We also meet the elders from both villages who put the girls forward for the bursary and will be doing the regular testing. These elders are solely responsible to report on the girls virginity status to the municipality, every varsity holiday. We also speak to Nomboniso Gasa, an author and professor on politics and gender studies. She feels that the intentions behind the bursary are good, but is strongly apposed to a woman’s virginity being aligned to her right to an education. She is also very concerned about this bursary in relation to the high cases of sexual assault on woman in South Africa. At the end of the piece the audience will have made an emotional connection with the girls who have received the bursary. They will have heard both what makes this a genius idea and how this is a step backwards for woman’s rights in South Africa. And then they can make their own minds up.
